what_its_for: Thyrotropin alfa is a man-made form of a hormone called TSH (thyroid-stimulating hormone). It is used in people who have had thyroid cancer. Your doctor will use it to help check if your thyroid cancer has come back, or to help a radioactive iodine treatment work better to destroy any remaining thyroid tissue after surgery.
how_to_take: This medicine is given as a shot (injection) into the muscle of your buttock (rear end). A healthcare provider in a clinic or hospital will give you this injection — you will NOT give it to yourself at home. You will usually receive two injections given 24 hours apart (one shot on Day 1 and another shot on Day 2). Any testing or treatment will happen after your last injection, usually on Day 3 or later.
dosing: The usual dose is 0.9 mg (milligrams) given as an injection into your muscle. You will receive this dose twice — once on Day 1 and once on Day 2 (about 24 hours apart). Your doctor will decide the exact schedule based on what the medicine is being used for.
missed_dose: Since this medicine is given by a healthcare provider in a clinical setting, it is important to keep all of your scheduled appointments. If you miss or need to reschedule an appointment, call your doctor or clinic right away. Do not try to reschedule on your own without talking to your care team, because the timing of this medicine is very important for your test or treatment to work correctly.
storage: You do not need to store this medicine at home. It is stored and prepared by healthcare professionals in a clinical or hospital setting. If for any reason you are given the medicine to hold temporarily, keep it refrigerated between 36°F and 46°F (2°C to 8°C) and do not freeze it. Keep it in its original packaging and away from light.
what_to_avoid: Talk to your doctor before receiving this medicine if you are pregnant or planning to become pregnant, as it may not be safe during pregnancy. Avoid making any changes to your thyroid medications without talking to your doctor first. Do not drive or operate heavy machinery if you feel dizzy, nauseated, or unwell after your injection until you feel better.
when_to_call_doctor: Call your doctor or seek emergency help right away if you experience any of the following after your injection: sudden severe headache, confusion, weakness or numbness on one side of your body, trouble speaking, vision changes (these could be signs of a stroke), chest pain, trouble breathing, severe allergic reaction (rash, hives, swelling of the face, lips, tongue, or throat, or difficulty breathing), severe nausea or vomiting that does not stop, or sudden worsening of symptoms if you have known spread of your thyroid cancer. Also call your doctor if you have any unusual swelling in your neck or throat, or if you feel very unwell after your shots.
when_it_works: Thyrotropin alfa works quickly — it raises TSH levels in your blood within about 24 hours of the first injection. Blood tests or radioactive iodine treatments are usually done within 24 to 72 hours after your second injection, when the medicine is working at its best. Your doctor will explain what to expect from your specific test or treatment results.
special_populations: Older adults (age 65 and older): This medicine has been used safely in older patients, but they may be at a slightly higher risk for side effects. Your doctor will monitor you closely. Kidney or liver problems: Tell your doctor if you have kidney or liver disease, as this may affect how your body processes the medicine. Pregnancy and breastfeeding: This medicine should generally not be used during pregnancy. If you are breastfeeding, talk to your doctor, as it is not fully known whether this medicine passes into breast milk. Children: The safety and effectiveness in children under 18 years old have not been fully established. Heart conditions: If you have heart disease or a history of stroke, tell your doctor before receiving this medicine, as there may be a slightly increased risk of complications.
